item.title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
item.dc:creator: Alex Benanti
item.description:
In Part 1, we saw that weighted Jacobi quickly damps oscillatory error but reduces smooth error very slowly. In this post, we will explore how coarse grids help address the error that relaxation leaves behind.

Recap and Motivation

Let us recall the 1D Poisson problem we saw in Part 1:

Take equal intervals, with and interior nodes for . The central difference method gives the discrete system:

with:

Let be the exact solution of this discrete system and its current iterative approximation. Define the algebraic error by ; this is distinct from the error caused by discretizing the PDE.

Also recall that, for a consistent linear stationary iterative method, we can represent the error after iterations as:

where is the error-propagation matrix and . If is diagonalizable, we can expand in its eigenvector basis and write:

This assumption holds for weighted Jacobi on our 1-D Poisson problem: its error-propagation matrix is symmetric. It does not hold for every stationary iteration.

The question that remains open from last time is: how do we remove the components of the error associated with eigenvalues for which —that is, the parts of the error that decay slowly?

Using Smoothing Effects

To address the low-frequency components of the error, we can use a “coarser” grid. A wave that is smooth relative to the fine-grid spacing varies more rapidly relative to the coarse-grid spacing. No new frequency information is created: we sample the same wave at fewer points. Here, coarsening means increasing the mesh spacing and reducing the number of interior unknowns.

But this sounds counterintuitive at first. Intuitively, you might assume that a coarser grid provides less usable detail—like watching a movie on a 1970s box TV instead of a modern IMAX screen. However, consider a broad, gentle slope spanning thousands of fine-grid pixels. To a local smoother inspecting adjacent pixels on the IMAX screen, that slope looks nearly flat, so the smoother barely adjusts it.

When we represent that same smooth error on a coarse grid, the spatial distance between grid points increases. Its physical shape does not change, but its variation from one grid point to the next becomes more pronounced. Some modes that relaxation handles poorly on the fine grid can therefore be reduced more effectively on a coarser grid. The smoothest modes may still need further coarsening. This is how I got myself to understand this nuanced idea, but an actual example may make it clearer.

Let us again consider the matrix . First, we will take , giving us the following frequencies/modes:

With the convention from Part 1, means eight grid intervals and seven interior unknowns. The eigenmodes are for .

Now consider : the grid spacing is , and there are three interior unknowns. The corresponding eigenmodes are for .

Of course, the plots look the same, but our evaluation points become fewer and farther apart. With this new discretization, remains a smooth mode, while modes and now become higher-frequency modes. But… why?

Why a Coarser Grid Helps

Let us consider the case from the previous example. The fine grid has spacing and intervals; the coarse grid has spacing and intervals. On the fine grid, this mode has components

Its dimensionless angular frequency is , so is its frequency relative to the grid’s Nyquist limit . This measures oscillation relative to the mesh spacing, not a fraction of the grid’s eigenmodes.

To isolate the sampling effect, retain every second fine-grid value (a transfer called injection). Coarse index corresponds to fine index , giving

The normalized frequency is now , at the start of the coarse grid’s high-frequency band. The physical wave has not changed; its angular frequency per grid step has doubled.

For weighted Jacobi with , the amplification factor for mode on a grid with intervals is

Thus , whereas . One sweep reduces this mode’s amplitude much more on the coarse grid. More generally, for . This smoothing statement is specific to the weighted-Jacobi choice above; ordinary Jacobi does not uniformly damp the high-frequency modes.

In the actual multigrid algorithm, we restrict the residual and solve a coarse error equation. Injection here illustrates the frequency change; the weighted restriction introduced below also changes the mode amplitudes.

What Happens to Fine High Frequencies?

What if we consider ? This mode is already high-frequency on the fine grid. Can its coarse samples distinguish it from every lower-frequency mode? (Try to answer this yourself.)

Answer in 3…2…1…

NO! The coarse grid has only three independent interior modes. The fine-grid mode becomes indistinguishable, up to a sign, from the coarse-grid mode. For , its samples are

Using the sine difference identity,

Hence . This is aliasing: different fine-grid modes give the same coarse samples up to a scalar factor.

More generally, for and ,

The boundary case is different: all its coarse samples are . The coarse grid therefore cannot represent every fine-grid error component independently. Notice also that an aliased mode need not be low-frequency on the coarse grid: in our example, is its highest mode.

This motivates the main idea behind multigrid methods:

  1. Use a few weighted-Jacobi sweeps on to reduce high-frequency error before transferring information to a coarser grid.

  2. Restrict the residual to and approximately solve the coarse error equation. Prolongate that correction to reduce error that was smooth on the fine grid.

  3. Apply the same idea recursively on , solving directly on the coarsest grid. Return through the levels with corrections and post-smoothing, then repeat cycles until the desired tolerance is reached. A finite number of sweeps does not generally eliminate all error exactly.

The Four Corners of Multigrid

NoteA note on the reference

The framework below draws on Olson (2015), particularly the discussion of smoothing, grid-transfer operators, and Galerkin coarse-grid correction. The author’s manuscript is freely available. I use different notation here: counts grid intervals, and denotes the coarsest mesh spacing.

Hierarchy of Grids

Let us assume that we have a hierarchy of grids. We start from the finest grid with a mesh size of . Then, the grid on the next level will have a mesh size of , the one after that , etc. For the coarsest grid, we denote it by (where is the number of levels we have). The physical grid at the finest level will be denoted as and is the grid at the coarsest level.

We choose nested grids so that each coarse node is a fine node. For the examples here, is a power of two and the coarsest grid has two intervals, leaving one interior unknown.

Interpolation/Prolongation

We have spoken much about these different grid discretizations, but we have yet to discuss how we actually TRANSFER between these discretizations. First, we will discuss the operator that brings us from a coarse grid to the finer grid at the next level up. This is called the interpolation/prolongation operator. It maps values defined on the coarse grid to values on the fine grid. For intervals and homogeneous Dirichlet boundary values, its action on the interior vectors is:

Then, for quantities and defined on grids and respectively, we can define the explicit prolongation as:

Designing prolongation matrices is a major research subfield of multigrid methods (to be discussed in later posts). For now, though, let us consider a simple example: linear interpolation.

At the even points on the fine grid, we copy the coarse values: for . At the odd points, we interpolate between adjacent coarse values. These are estimates of the missing values, not a recovery of arbitrary fine-grid data. Linear interpolation gives:

With , the matrix acting on the interior values for and is:

Restriction

The operator that transfers fine-grid values to the coarse grid is called restriction. For the same interior vector spaces, it has the mapping:

More specifically, we can write the restriction as:

As with prolongation, there are many restriction operators. Here we choose transpose restriction, , which is commonly paired with the Galerkin coarse operator . Restriction alone is not the Galerkin projection. Using our prolongation matrix gives:

The weights here are , a weighted sum. The common 1-D full-weighting choice instead uses , with weights . We use transpose restriction throughout this post, including the code. With either convention, form both the coarse matrix and the coarse right-hand side consistently. Multiplying both by the same nonzero scalar leaves the exact coarse correction unchanged.

Iterative Methods and the Two-Grid Scheme

We have already discussed iterative methods a bit, but some additional context is needed to better understand how they fit into the entire “multigrid” story. On the finest grid we solve for the solution; on coarser grids we approximately solve error equations. You may or may not know, from numerical linear algebra, that one way we can find crude approximations to the solutions of linear systems is through iterative methods (as was discussed a bit in Part 1). Let’s say, for example, we had a simple two-grid scheme. That is, we have a single fine grid and a single coarse grid. Then, the algorithm would proceed as follows:

With our error convention, and satisfy . This explains why we solve for a coarse error correction and add its prolongation to the current approximation.

  1. Iterate on the fine-level problem to reach via a few iterations of an iterative method like weighted Jacobi or Gauss-Seidel.

  2. Restrict the residual to the coarse grid by applying a designated restriction operator:

  3. Solve the coarse approximation to the error equation, with homogeneous boundary values:

  4. Prolongate the coarse correction and update the fine approximation:

  5. Apply a few more smoothing sweeps to , starting from the corrected .

Note: You may be wondering: how do we find ? It turns out, we RAP! Not in the Kendrick Lamar way, but the “let’s restrict and prolongate our fine-level discretization” way. More specifically, we have:

For our fine-grid finite-difference matrix and linear interpolation, the choice gives , where is obtained by directly discretizing on spacing . Full weighting would give itself. This scaling does not change weighted-Jacobi’s error-propagation matrix, since its diagonal scales by the same factor.

Here is symmetric positive definite and has full column rank, so is invertible. For and an exact coarse solve, the fine-space operator is the Galerkin projection onto the range of , orthogonal in the inner product. The error after correction is . This precisely removes errors in that coarse space, but not arbitrary fine-grid errors.

Multigrid Scheme

A convergent two-grid method can reach the desired algebraic accuracy, but its coarse solve may still be expensive on a large problem. Multigrid addresses that cost by approximately solving the coarse error equation with another two-grid scheme, and repeating this recursively until the coarsest problem is small. Hence multigrid (finally)! One way to organize this recursion is a V-cycle: visit each coarser grid once, then return through the finer grids, correcting and smoothing along the way.

NoteAlgorithm: one multigrid V-cycle

Input: current mesh spacing , right-hand side , and initial approximation .

Setup: choose smoothing counts and construct the grid hierarchy, transfer operators, and coarse matrices in advance. Write this routine as .

  1. Coarsest grid: if , solve directly and return .

  2. Pre-smooth: apply relaxation sweeps to , starting from the current .

  3. Compute and restrict the residual:

  4. Recurse on the coarse error equation, starting from zero:

  5. Prolongate and correct:

  6. Post-smooth: apply relaxation sweeps to , starting from the corrected approximation.

  7. Return the updated .

To solve the original problem, repeat V-cycles on the finest grid until or a chosen maximum number of cycles is reached. The coarse calls solve for an error correction, so they use homogeneous boundary conditions for this Dirichlet problem.

Watching a V-Cycle

The animation follows one cycle through six levels, from to . On the way down, we smooth and restrict the residual. On the way up, we prolongate the error correction and smooth again. The highlighted node marks the current stage; the notches show its grid. This is an illustration of the traversal, not a plot of error magnitude.

Computational Experiment

For a concrete version of our Poisson problem, take

whose exact solution is . The code below starts from zero on a grid with intervals and applies V-cycles until the relative residual is below . Each cycle uses two weighted-Jacobi sweeps before and after the coarse correction, with .

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def hierarchy(n):
    """Interior Dirichlet matrices and linear transfer operators."""
    if n < 2 or n & (n - 1):
        raise ValueError("n must be a power of two, at least 2")
    A = n**2 * (2 * np.eye(n - 1)
                 - np.eye(n - 1, k=1) - np.eye(n - 1, k=-1))
    matrices, transfers = [A], []
    while n > 2:
        P = np.zeros((n - 1, n // 2 - 1))
        for col in range(P.shape[1]):
            P[2 * col:2 * col + 3, col] = [0.5, 1, 0.5]
        R = P.T
        matrices.append(R @ matrices[-1] @ P)
        transfers.append(P)
        n //= 2
    return matrices, transfers


def smooth(A, b, v, sweeps=2, omega=2/3):
    for _ in range(sweeps):
        v = v + omega * (b - A @ v) / np.diag(A)
    return v


def v_cycle(matrices, transfers, level, b, v):
    A = matrices[level]
    if level == len(matrices) - 1:
        return np.linalg.solve(A, b)
    v = smooth(A, b, v)
    P = transfers[level]
    coarse_rhs = P.T @ (b - A @ v)
    coarse_error = v_cycle(matrices, transfers, level + 1,
                           coarse_rhs, np.zeros_like(coarse_rhs))
    v = v + P @ coarse_error
    return smooth(A, b, v)


n = 64
x = np.linspace(0, 1, n + 1)
b = np.pi**2 * np.sin(np.pi * x[1:-1])
matrices, transfers = hierarchy(n)
A = matrices[0]
v = np.zeros(n - 1)
relative_residuals = [np.linalg.norm(b - A @ v) / np.linalg.norm(b)]

for cycle in range(50):
    v = v_cycle(matrices, transfers, 0, b, v)
    relative_residuals.append(np.linalg.norm(b - A @ v) / np.linalg.norm(b))
    if relative_residuals[-1] < 1e-10:
        break
else:
    raise RuntimeError("V-cycles did not reach the residual tolerance")

# Check the iterative result against a direct solve of the same discrete system.
np.testing.assert_allclose(v, np.linalg.solve(A, b), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-11)
print(f"V-cycles: {len(relative_residuals) - 1}")
print(f"Final relative residual: {relative_residuals[-1]:.2e}")
print(f"Maximum error against sin(pi*x): {np.max(np.abs(v - np.sin(np.pi*x[1:-1]))):.2e}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.4))
xx = np.linspace(0, 1, 500)
axes[0].plot(xx, np.sin(np.pi * xx), color="#8a8a8a", label="Exact solution")
axes[0].plot(x, np.r_[0, v, 0], ".", color="#235789", label="Multigrid")
axes[0].set(xlabel="x", ylabel="u(x)")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
axes[1].semilogy(range(len(relative_residuals)), relative_residuals,
                 "o-", color="#235789", markersize=4)
axes[1].set(xlabel="Completed V-cycles", ylabel="Relative residual")
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.set_facecolor("none")
fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
plt.rcParams["savefig.transparent"] = True
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
V-cycles: 10
Final relative residual: 4.26e-11
Maximum error against sin(pi*x): 2.01e-04

The residual measures how well we solve the discrete system. Its convergence does not remove the finite-difference discretization error, which is why the error against remains larger. This compact example uses dense matrices for readability; a large multigrid solver would use sparse matrices or stencil operations.

Closing Thoughts

Congrats! Now you can brag to your friends and family that you know what all the kids are talking about: multigrid methods. Still, this short series was just a primer on this subfield of numerical analysis, and there is much left unsaid about more “sophisticated” versions of this idea. However, they all rest on the same principles we discussed in these two posts. In future posts, I hope to delve deeper into multigrid and even talk about “neural” multigrid methods (one of my primary research interests).

References

Olson, Luke. 2015. “Multigrid Methods: Geometric.” In Encyclopedia of Applied and Computational Mathematics. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-70529-1_338.

item.description:
This will be the first blog post in a two-part introduction to multigrid. For those of you who are new to numerical linear algebra, you are certainly welcome to read as I have designed these posts for those who are unfamiliar with numerical methods entirely! However, you may have a greater appreciation for what is being discussed if you are at least familiar with Jacobi/Gauss-Seidel iteration. The only “hard” prerequisites are an understanding of linear algebra (specifically eigenvalue problems and bases) and calculus.

Motivation

While multigrid is considered a numerical linear algebra technique, it was originally developed for finding numerical solutions of PDEs. So, we will use a boundary value problem (BVP) to help us understand how multigrid works, why it’s so helpful, and how it can be generalized.

Suppose we want to find the numerical solution to the following BVP:

As it turns out, we don’t call this an elliptic PDE for no reason. As a fun side exercise, maybe try to figure out why this family of PDEs may be called “elliptic” :). However, I don’t want to get too far off track here. The reason I want to distinguish this family of PDEs is because this was the family of PDEs for which multigrid was originally designed.

item.title: What Is a PDE?
item.dc:creator: Alex Benanti
item.description:
If your physics knowledge comes mostly from brilliant communicators like Neil deGrasse Tyson or Brian Cox, you aren’t alone. However, while pop science is fantastic for sparking curiosity, it rarely gives you the tools to look under the hood yourself. To really understand the universe—and eventually, to teach machine learning models how to simulate it—we have to speak its native language: Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). I know that term can be a massive mental barrier. If you’ve had bad experiences with math in the past, PDEs can sound incredibly intimidating. My goal in this first post is to completely demystify them. If you have a basic grasp of limits and derivatives, you have everything you need to follow along.

Partial Derivatives

Let be a function of two variables. We can take a derivative with respect to one variable, while the other is held constant. These are the partial derivatives, or partials, of .

In practical terms, if describes a surface, then measures how the surface changes as we move in the -direction while keeping fixed. Similarly, measures the change in the -direction while is fixed.

Example

Suppose we have the function:

Differentiating with respect to and holding constant gives us:

while differentiating with respect to and holding constant gives us:

Definition of a PDE

A PDE is a relationship between an unknown function of at least two variables, its partials, and functions of the independent variables. The order of a PDE is the highest derivative appearing.

More formally, a PDE is an equation of the form:

where are the independent variables, is the unknown function (also called the dependent variable) that depends on these variables, and represent the partial derivatives of with respect to the independent variables. Note that we do not stop at order two in the general case. Higher-order PDEs occur as well, although first- and second-order equations are the most common examples in an introductory course.

Examples

  1. Transport Equation

  1. Laplace’s Equation

  1. Heat Equation

Note that for the heat equation, although it contains only a first derivative with respect to time, it is second order because is a second derivative.

What Does it Mean to Solve a PDE?

For now, we will use the “classical” notion of a solution. A sufficiently differentiable function solves a PDE on a domain if substituting and its partial derivatives into the equation makes the equation true at every point in . If the problem also includes initial or boundary conditions, then must satisfy those conditions as well.

Example

Does solve ? Let’s find out!

So, we can verify that this particular solves the given PDE! (If you look closely, you can verify that this is a variation of the heat equation with diffusivity ). Well, that wasn’t so bad… is this really all physicists do? Well, as it turns out, checking if a given function is a solution to a PDE is much more straightforward than actually finding solutions. And “the solution” is perhaps an improper phrase to use. A PDE by itself often has an infinite number of solutions. Initial and boundary conditions help determine which solution describes the particular situation we care about. Even after initial and boundary conditions are supplied, many PDE problems do not have a useful closed-form solution. In those cases, numerical methods allow us to approximate the solution on a computer.

Everything I just said will make more sense in future blog posts, but it should be well-established that the process of finding solutions to PDEs is not as straightforward as finding solutions to algebraic equations you may have dealt with in the past. This is not to say it is more difficult, but it certainly requires a different approach.

Some unanswered questions go deeper than finding a convenient closed-form formula. In certain cases, fundamental questions about the existence and regularity of solutions remain unresolved. A famous example is the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes system. The associated Millennium Prize Problem asks, roughly speaking, whether smooth solutions arising from suitable smooth initial data always remain smooth for all time, or whether they can develop singularities (Fefferman 2006). As of July 2026, the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved, with 1 million US dollars allocated to its solution (Clay Mathematics Institute, n.d.).

Optional Deep Dive: Derivation of a 1D Wave Equation

To cap off this first post, I would like to do a derivation relating to physics so that you can see how valuable PDEs are for modelling the world around us. To fully follow along with this derivation, I recommend the reader also have some knowledge of antiderivatives and integration as well as Newton’s second law.

Suppose an elastic string of length has both ends tied down and is subject to transverse waves. Let denote the vertical displacement of the string at horizontal position and time . Assume that the string has uniform linear mass density , measured in kg/m, and that its motion is purely transverse. Because the endpoints are fixed, we have:

Further, we assume that its slope is small in magnitude (), and damping and external forces are neglected.

Now, we can zoom in and pick two distinct points on the string and . At the endpoints of this segment, the tangent to the string makes angles and with the horizontal. The corresponding tension magnitudes are and respectively:

Now, we have to balance the forces. Since there is no horizontal acceleration (the string only vibrates) the forces will add up to zero.

However, there is a vertical acceleration. So, we can obtain the total vertical force using Newton’s second law , where the vertical acceleration of the string is . Between points and , we can take the integral of mass density times acceleration to give us the net vertical force:

Now, using the right triangle that is formed by the angle and vertical change (demonstrated above) we can observe that:

Under the small-slope assumption, , we approximate the and values as:

Takeaway

A PDE is not merely an equation containing unusual derivative symbols. It is a local rule describing how a quantity changes with respect to multiple independent variables—often space and time. Together with appropriate initial and/or boundary conditions, that rule can become a mathematical model of a physical system.

We have not yet solved the wave equation—or any other PDE in a systematic way. That is where the next parts of this series will lead: first toward analytical methods, then numerical approximation, and eventually toward the ways scientific machine learning can learn from or work alongside these equations.
